guide_intro.title: Gastown local
lines: Waterfront's right here. SeaBus, SkyTrain, West Coast Express: pick your adventure.
Head toward Water Street if you want the old brick and a ridiculous number of clock photos.
You're on the unceded territories of the Musqueam, Squamish, and Tsleil-Waututh Nations.
In the morning this end of the route still feels half commuter corridor, half heritage reveal — you can watch office workers peel away while visitors are only just orienting themselves.
From Maple Tree Square the district reads less like a single story and more like a layered meeting point shaped by routes, shoreline change, and public memory.
Now that you have logged all three observations, the neighbourhood starts to connect through details instead of a single landmark.

busker_clock_corner.title: Street band
lines: One review said Gastown was nothing but souvenir shops and an underwhelming clock.
Cool, I'm providing the deluxe soundtrack for free. Tips accepted.
At least my set lasts longer than the steam.
The clock can whistle in the rain. My amp is filing a complaint.
Even the bad reviews admit the bricks photograph well at dusk.

pedestrian_route_tip.title: Water Street walker
lines: Water Street's just down there. It's better on foot, honestly.
Keep an eye out for deliveries and people suddenly stopping for photos.
If you miss the clock, just follow the crowd looking up.
Morning walkers move like they already know where every curb cut and shortcut is, which makes the block feel like a lived-in route rather than a set piece.
When fog settles in, everyone shortens their stride and pays more attention to the storefront light and the next patch of sidewalk ahead.

pedestrian_clock_hint.title: Gastown passerby
lines: Locals don't usually schedule their day around the Steam Clock. Tourists do.
Somebody was mad it's from 1977. Sorry it wasn't forged by a Victorian wizard.
Water Street's the good bit. Keep walking.
Closer to the Steam Clock, the flow changes every few seconds — somebody stops for a photo, somebody slips around them, and the whole street recomposes itself.
Once you have stepped into Maple Tree Square, the clock feels less like a lone attraction and more like one actor in a bigger street scene.

tourist_clock_stop.title: Tourist
lines: I waited fifteen minutes for a clock to do a small toot.
Honestly, I've paid more for worse entertainment.
My review: three stars. One for each minute I spent explaining it to my family.
Five hundred people here to photograph an object that literally tells them when to go home.
I still took twelve photos. Obviously.
One star. It steamed, I steamed, and then it rained on my pastry.
Wait, I thought the clock was the whole attraction. There are more streets?

tourist_clock_photo.title: Street photographer
lines: Could everyone stop standing in front of the famous tiny clock?
I've got forty-seven photos of strangers' jackets and half a whistle.
Five stars for the brickwork, though. It knows its angles.
The fog makes my photo look like a period drama about disappointing clocks.
Someone reviewed the clock as 'too crowded'. Sir, you are also the crowd.

skateboarder_corridor.title: Gastown skateboarder
lines: Some tourist complained about the cobblestones. As a skateboarder, I actually have notes.
This entire street is one giant vibration setting.
Clock's fine though. Very committed to standing still.
At night the corridor opens up and the sound of wheels carries farther, so you feel every seam in the paving and every pocket of people ahead.
When the street goes wet, everybody rolling through has to read the bricks, the metal covers, and the tourist stops way earlier.

cyclist_water_street.title: Gastown cyclist
lines: Someone reviewed Gastown as too busy. They arrived on a cruise ship.
I am begging everyone to look up from the camera before stepping into the street.
Also, whoever designed the cobblestones has clearly never ridden a bike.
Morning makes this stretch feel more utilitarian — delivery workers, commuters, and early walkers all negotiate the same narrow line.
Near the clock I feather the pace because somebody is always drifting backward into the lane to get the whole landmark in frame.
If you already spotted the painted wall detail, you have probably noticed how the quieter walls pull people a block farther than the famous clock does.

parking_small_talk.title: Station East walker
lines: Someone left a one-star review because the Steam Clock was... a clock.
Mate, it whistles and shoots steam. The rest is your emotional journey.
Anyway, SeaBus is right there and the harbour view's free. Give the mountains five stars.
A tourist said Gastown was damp. In Vancouver. In November.
I'm forwarding their review directly to the clouds.
Apparently the clock is underwhelming at night too. I dunno, the harbour lights are doing all the heavy lifting.

parking_high_five.title: Friendly stranger
lines: A reviewer said this city wasn't friendly. High five to dispute that?
Five stars for the interaction. Zero stars for the parking situation.
Someone gave the rain two stars. That's honestly generous.
High five before my sleeve becomes a sponge?
A high five? Quick, before both our SkyTrains leave.
